seeds.goal: You can examine a contested question at length: frame it precisely, develop competing positions on their strongest form, and arrive at a qualified position of your own.

seeds.task: Write a discursive essay (280–320 words) on whether automation threatens employment: define the terms, develop the strongest case on each side, identify what the disagreement actually turns on, and give a qualified conclusion.
model: Debates about automation and employment usually founder on a conflation: 'work' can mean the tasks a job contains or the institution through which income and status are distributed, and the evidence points in different directions for each.

The case for optimism is historical and strong: every previous wave of mechanisation destroyed identifiable occupations while raising aggregate employment, because falling prices raised demand elsewhere faster than machines displaced labour.
Weaving is the standard example, and the standard example is accurate: employment in textiles rose for decades after the power loom.

The pessimistic case does not deny this; it denies that the mechanism transfers. Earlier machines substituted for muscle and left judgement alone, whereas current systems substitute for the routine cognitive work that has absorbed displaced labour every previous time.
Identify what the disagreement turns on
The disagreement therefore turns on a single empirical question: whether the tasks being automated now are the ones that historically provided the landing ground.
There is a further consideration that neither camp emphasises: even a transition that ends well distributes its costs badly, and the population that bears them is not the population that gains.
My own position is therefore split. On aggregate employment I find the optimistic case more persuasive, largely because its mechanism has been observed and the pessimistic one is inferred.
State the limit of your conclusion

On the experience of the two decades in which the adjustment happens, I find it irrelevant: an argument that ends well over fifty years is not an answer to somebody who has thirty of them left to work.

seeds.goal: You can write a proposal that survives a committee: state the decision sought, the case, the cost, the risks and the reason the alternative is worse.
seeds.why: Committees reject proposals for procedural reasons: no decision requested, no cost, no owner. A good idea is not enough.
seeds.ex: Nurlan's proposal named the decision required in the first line. It was approved without amendment.
seeds.read: Read the proposal and find one thing: what exactly is the committee being asked to approve?
seeds.task: Write a proposal (260–300 words) to a committee: the decision sought, the problem with evidence, the proposal, the cost, the risks with mitigations, why the alternative is worse and the timetable.
model: The committee is asked to approve the reallocation of 1.2 million tenge from the equipment reserve to a two-year mentoring post, and to review the post in June 2027.

Withdrawal from the foundation programme has risen from 9 to 21 per cent over three cohorts. Exit interviews attribute this overwhelmingly to the first six weeks rather than to academic difficulty later.

The pattern is consistent with a structural gap rather than with selection: the students who leave are not those with the weakest entry scores, but those with no prior contact with anybody who has studied here.

The proposal is to fund one full-time mentoring post responsible for structured contact with every foundation student in weeks one to six, and for the referral of any student who misses two consecutive sessions.
The cost is 1.2 million tenge over two years, comprising salary at 45,000 tenge a month, a small training budget and no additional space requirement.

Two risks are material. First, the post may become an administrative role; this is mitigated by defining the referral duty in the job description and reporting monthly on contacts made rather than on hours worked. Second, the effect may not be measurable in one cohort; the review date is therefore set after two.
Explain why the alternative is worse

The alternative under discussion — distributing the duty across existing tutors — has been tried in two departments, where recorded contact fell to a third of the intended level within a term, for the predictable reason that a duty owned by everyone is owned by nobody.
If approved in March, the post can be advertised in April and filled before the September intake; a decision after May makes the first cohort unreachable.

seeds.goal: You can review a work critically: reconstruct its argument faithfully, test it at its weakest joint, credit what survives and place it in its field.
seeds.why: A critical review is not a negative one. The discipline is to make the work's case better than the work did, then say where it breaks.
seeds.ex: Damir's review reconstructed a book's argument in three sentences before attacking it. The journal published it.
seeds.read: Read the review and find one thing: which step in the argument does the reviewer identify as the weak one?
seeds.task: Write a critical review (260–300 words) of a non-fiction book: reconstruct its argument, test the weakest step, credit what survives, place it in its field and give a judgement.
model: Sennett's 'The Craftsman' belongs to a line of argument that runs from Ruskin onward, and it inherits both the strength and the vulnerability of that tradition.

The argument, stripped to its joints, runs: skill is developed through resistance; resistance requires material that pushes back; therefore forms of work that remove resistance — scripted, automated, monitored — degrade the capacity they appear to support.

The middle step is the book's real contribution, and it is supported by material that most writers on work never touch: apprenticeship records, the physical vocabulary of the workshop, the timing of a hand movement learned over years.

The first step is where the argument is thinnest. 'Resistance' is used to cover phenomena that behave differently: the resistance of a material, the resistance of a difficult colleague and the resistance of an arbitrary rule are treated as if the same skill answered all three.
That elision matters, because the political conclusion depends on it: if the third kind of resistance does not build skill, then a great deal of what the book defends is merely unpleasant.
The book is also uneven in evidence: chapters built on historical record are precise, whereas those on contemporary work rest on interviews reported without number or method.
What survives is substantial: the account of how tacit knowledge is transmitted, and the observation that institutions optimise for what they can measure and thereby remove what they cannot.
As a philosophical essay it is better than its reception suggested; as an argument about contemporary labour it needs the empirical chapter it does not contain.

seeds.goal: You can summarise a demanding text accurately and respond to it in its own terms: agree, dispute and extend, without misrepresenting the original.

seeds.task: Write a summary and response (260–300 words) to an argument that cities should abolish parking minimums: summarise it faithfully, agree with something on its own grounds, dispute something specific, extend one point and conclude.
model: Name the text and the claim

In 'The High Cost of Free Parking', the argument is that minimum parking requirements are a hidden tax: they force every building to subsidise driving, and the cost appears in rents paid by people who may not own a car.

The mechanism given is precise. A requirement of one space per unit adds a fixed cost per unit; that cost is unbundled from the car and bundled into the rent, so the tenant pays whether or not the space is used.
From this the author derives the observed pattern: abundant parking, high rents, and a built environment shaped by a standard that no city has ever demonstrated to be correct.

The core of this is difficult to resist. The requirements were set by copying, not by measurement, and the copying is documented: identical ratios appear in cities with radically different transport systems.

The disputable step is the transition to policy. Abolishing minimums removes a distortion, but in a city where the street is unpriced it converts a private cost into a public one: what was a garage becomes a queue for kerb space.
The cities that abolished minimums without pricing the kerb — and several did — recorded exactly this, and the ones that did both did not.
Extend a point rather than disputing it

The argument can also be extended in a direction the author does not take: the same logic applies to any requirement bundled into rent, including standards written for a household size that most cities no longer have.

The conclusion should therefore be sequenced rather than softened: price the kerb, then abolish the minimum. In that order the argument holds; in the reverse order it produces the outcome its critics predict and its author does not want.

seeds.goal: You can write a policy brief: state the issue, the options with costs and consequences, the recommendation and what would falsify it.

seeds.task: Write a policy brief (260–300 words): the issue in one paragraph, the current position, two options with costs and consequences, a recommendation, implementation and what would falsify it.
model: Put the whole argument in the first paragraph

Rural school transport currently funds vehicles rather than journeys. Reallocating the same budget to a per-journey subsidy would extend service to 38 settlements now unserved, at no additional cost, while reducing the fleet by roughly a fifth. The main risk is a transitional gap of one term.
Twenty-two per cent of rural students travel more than one hour each way, and the correlation between journey time and withdrawal after year 9 is strong and stable across four years of data.
The current model allocates buses by settlement size. This produces near-empty vehicles on some routes and none at all on routes below the threshold, regardless of how many students would use them.
Give the first option with cost
The first option is to lower the threshold. This is administratively trivial and costs approximately 340 million tenge a year, because it multiplies the same inefficiency across more routes.
Give the second option with cost

The second is to fund journeys rather than vehicles: contracting local operators per verified student journey, at a ceiling per kilometre, with the school confirming attendance. Modelled on existing route data, this covers all 38 settlements within the current allocation.
The second option is recommended, principally because it makes the cost proportional to use rather than to geography, and because it can be reversed within one contract cycle if it fails.

Implementation requires a verification mechanism that does not create a new administrative post: attendance is already recorded electronically, and the same record can be used, provided it is not made a payment condition for the school itself.
Say what would show it is wrong

The recommendation should be abandoned if, in the pilot, verified journeys exceed the modelled figure by more than fifteen per cent, since that would indicate either fraud or a demand estimate that cannot be funded.

seeds.goal: You can write an op-ed: open on a concrete image, make one argument, give the opposition its due and end on a line that carries the point.

model: The pharmacy in Zharkent that closed in March had a handwritten sign in the window for six weeks: 'Insulin — ask at the shop next door.'
It was the fourth closure in the district in two years, and in each case the same sign appeared, because the shop next door is not licensed to hold insulin and everybody knew it.

The regulation that closed these pharmacies was not aimed at them. It raised the minimum floor area and staffing for licensed premises, in response to a genuine problem in cities, and it was applied uniformly to a country where uniformity is the problem.

Since 2022, urban pharmacy numbers have been stable while rural ones have fallen by 17 per cent, and the fall is concentrated entirely below a population threshold that the regulation does not mention but effectively defines.
The rule exists for a reason that is not trivial: unqualified dispensing killed people, and the cases that produced the regulation were not hypothetical.

But a rule that removes the pharmacy entirely does not raise the standard of dispensing in Zharkent; it moves dispensing to the shop next door, where there is no standard at all, and calls the result compliance.

The remedy is not deregulation but a differentiated licence: fewer square metres, the same qualification requirement, and a supervising pharmacist responsible for several sites, which is how three neighbouring countries handle exactly this.

A regulation should be judged by what it produces, not by what it prohibits. In Zharkent, it produced a handwritten sign.

seeds.goal: You can write a full report: terms of reference, method, findings, analysis and recommendations that follow visibly from the evidence.

seeds.task: Write a report with recommendations (280–320 words): terms of reference, method with limitations, three findings with data, analysis, and recommendations linked to specific findings.
model: This report was commissioned by the Faculty Board on 12 January to establish why completion rates on the part-time programme have fallen and to recommend measures within existing resources.
Describe the method and its limits

The analysis draws on enrolment records for six cohorts, a survey of 214 current and former students (response rate 58 per cent) and eleven semi-structured interviews. Former students who left before the second semester are under-represented, which almost certainly understates the problems reported.
First, the fall is not general: completion on the evening pathway has been stable at 71–74 per cent, while the weekend pathway has fallen from 68 to 49 per cent in three years.

Second, withdrawal on the weekend pathway is concentrated in the four weeks after the first assessment, and the survey associates this with the timing of feedback rather than with the mark received: median return time is nineteen days.

Third, the two modules with the highest withdrawal are also the two taught by staff who teach on both pathways in the same week; interviews suggest scheduling rather than teaching quality as the mechanism.

Taken together, these point to a structural problem in one pathway rather than to student capability. A programme that returns feedback after the next assessment has begun does not give a working adult the information they need to decide whether to continue.
It is recommended (from Finding 2) that feedback on the first assessment be returned within seven days on the weekend pathway, with a reduced marking load for that assessment only.

It is further recommended (from Findings 1 and 3) that the two affected modules be scheduled in alternate terms across pathways, and that completion be reviewed by pathway rather than in aggregate from this year.

seeds.goal: You can write a statement for a competitive application: show intellectual development through specific work, name what you found difficult and connect it to what you want to study.

model: I became interested in economics through a question I could not answer: why the bread in our district costs the same in eleven shops and different in the twelfth.
I spent two months recording prices in those twelve shops and mapping them against distance from the wholesale market, opening hours and whether the shop was part of a chain.

The pattern was not the one I expected. Distance explained almost nothing; what predicted the outlier was whether the owner also owned the building, which changed the rent from a cost into a decision.
It took me three weeks to see this, because I had begun by assuming that price is set by cost, and my data kept refusing to say so.
Connect to wider reading, with criticism
That failure sent me to industrial organisation, and specifically to the literature on price rigidity, which I found more persuasive on why prices do not move than on why particular firms deviate.
Show what you know you lack
I am aware that my project would not survive a serious methodological question: twelve shops is not a sample, and I chose the variables I could observe rather than the ones that matter.
Connect to what you want to study
That is precisely why I want to study econometrics rather than to read more economics: the constraint on my thinking is not ideas but the ability to test them.
Say what you want to work on
I would like to work eventually on prices in thin markets — the small settlements where competition is a theoretical concept and the nearest alternative is forty kilometres away.

seeds.goal: You can compare two cases analytically: build a frame that applies to both, use it consistently, and draw a conclusion that neither case alone would support.
seeds.why: Comparison earns its place only when it produces something new. If the essay could be split in two without loss, the comparison was decorative.
seeds.ex: Dana compared two housing programmes through one variable. Her tutor called the frame 'the actual contribution'.
seeds.read: Read the essay and find one thing: what conclusion does the comparison support that neither case alone would?
seeds.task: Write a comparative essay (280–320 words) comparing two policies or programmes: establish an analytical frame, apply it to both, identify where they diverge and why, and conclude something neither case alone would show.
model: Both the Vienna and the Singapore housing systems are described as public success stories, and both are usually explained by their scale. The more useful comparison is by tenure: what a resident owns, and therefore what they can lose.
Apply the frame to the first case

Vienna's model rests on regulated rental: the city or a limited-profit association owns the stock, the resident holds a secure tenancy, and the price is set against costs rather than against the market.
The consequence is a system whose political support comes from the middle of the income distribution, because access is not restricted to the poor and the rent advantage is visible every month.
Apply the frame to the second case
Singapore inverts this: residents purchase long leases, subsidised at the point of sale, and the state retains the land.

The political support here is even stronger, but it is of a different kind: it is the support of owners for an asset, which makes the system extremely stable and extremely difficult to adjust downwards.
Identify where they diverge and why

The two diverge sharply under one condition — a period of falling prices. Vienna's residents lose nothing they hold; Singapore's face a loss on the largest asset most households own, which converts a housing policy into a savings policy and constrains every subsequent decision.
This is visible in what each system finds impossible: Vienna struggles to expand supply quickly; Singapore cannot let prices fall.
Conclude what only the comparison shows
What the comparison shows, and neither case alone does, is that the durability of a housing system depends less on how it is financed than on what it makes residents afraid of.

seeds.goal: You can write an abstract: state the question, the method, the findings and the contribution in a fixed, dense form.
seeds.why: An abstract is read by a committee comparing sixty of them. Vagueness in any of the four moves is fatal.
seeds.ex: Askar's abstract stated its result rather than promising one. It was accepted for a graduate conference.
seeds.read: Read the abstract and find one thing: what is the finding, stated as a result rather than a promise?
seeds.task: Write a conference abstract (180–220 words): the gap or question, the data and method, the finding stated as a result, the contribution and one limitation.
model: Establish the context in one sentence
Studies of language shift in Central Asia have concentrated on urban populations, where reported language use is easiest to collect.
The rural picture is largely inferred from these data, although the mechanisms usually proposed — schooling, media, mobility — differ substantially outside cities.
This paper asks whether the reported urban pattern of generational shift holds in settlements below 5,000 inhabitants.

It draws on 1,240 household interviews conducted in 2023 across four regions, combined with school enrolment records for the same settlements, and uses a mixed-effects model with settlement as a random effect.
State the finding as a result

The generational pattern does not hold. In settlements with a functioning secondary school, shift is slower by roughly a generation; in settlements where children board elsewhere from age twelve, it is faster than the urban baseline.
This suggests that the operative variable is not exposure to the majority language but the age at which a child leaves the household, which no current model treats as central.
The paper's contribution is therefore to identify boarding rather than schooling as the mechanism, and to provide the first settlement-level estimates for the region.
The design is cross-sectional; a longitudinal test of the boarding hypothesis is proposed but not conducted here.

seeds.why: An executive summary is not an introduction. It must be complete on its own, because for most readers it will be the entire document.

seeds.read: Read the summary and find one thing: what decision is being recommended?

The site handles 4 per cent of volume at 11 per cent of network cost, and the gap has widened in each of the last six quarters.
The cost structure is fixed rather than variable: rent, two shifts of staffing and a minimum vehicle allocation are incurred whether the site handles four hundred parcels a day or forty.
Volume has fallen 38 per cent since 2022, driven by two contract losses that have not been replaced, while the cost per parcel has risen from 340 to 610 tenge against a network average of 290.
Closure saves an estimated 41 million tenge a year net of the additional Astana run, with a one-off cost of 6 million in redundancy and lease exit.

seeds.goal: You can respond to public criticism of your work: state what the critic is right about, isolate the disagreement, answer it with evidence and leave the exchange usable.
seeds.why: This genre is a test of temperament as much as of argument. The reader is judging whether you are safe to disagree with.

seeds.read: Read the response and find one thing: which criticism does the writer accept?

model: I am grateful to Dr Amanova for a response that engages with the argument rather than with its conclusion.
She is right that the 2019 figures are not comparable with the later series: the definition of a 'rural school' changed in 2020, and I should have said so in the text rather than in a footnote.
She is also right that the effect I report is small in absolute terms, and that I described it in language that implied more than the size warrants.

The disagreement is narrower than the response suggests, and it concerns one step: whether the fall in enrolment after consolidation reflects families leaving the district or families choosing a different school within it.

The response treats these as indistinguishable in the data. They are separable, and I separated them: district-level population records show no corresponding out-migration in the three years following consolidation in seven of the nine cases.

What those records cannot show is timing within a year, which is a real limitation and the reason my claim is stated as a probability rather than as a finding.

The question is answerable. Enrolment records held at settlement level would settle it in either direction, and I would be glad to work on them jointly rather than to continue this in print.

seeds.goal: You can make a formal request that carries its own justification: state it, ground it in rule or precedent, pre-empt the standard refusal and offer a fallback.

model: I am writing to request that my thesis submission deadline be extended from 30 May to 27 June, a period of four weeks.

Regulation 14.3 provides for an extension of up to eight weeks where a documented interruption affects a period of active research, and specifies that the extension should reflect the period lost rather than the delay experienced.

Between 2 and 27 April I was unable to access the laboratory following its closure for electrical work; the closure was unannounced and the department's own notice of 4 April is attached, together with my supervisor's confirmation that the affected experiments could not be run elsewhere.
The period lost was twenty-five days. I am requesting twenty-eight, of which three account for the re-preparation of samples that had to be discarded.

seeds.goal: You can write an editorial: speak for a publication rather than for yourself, take a position with evidence and address those who can act.
seeds.why: An editorial has no 'I'. Its authority comes from the paper, which means the evidence has to carry weight the writer's personality cannot.
seeds.ex: The student paper's editorial on assessment deadlines was answered formally by the dean.
seeds.read: Read the editorial and find one thing: who is being asked to act, and what exactly are they asked to do?

model: The faculty announced last week that resit examinations will move from September to July, with three weeks' notice to students already registered.
The change is defensible; the notice is not, and the two should not be confused in the discussion that follows.
Give the case for the change

There is a real argument for a July resit: a student who fails in June currently waits eleven weeks, and the evidence from two comparable faculties suggests that pass rates rise when the gap is shorter.
Give the case against the timing

The difficulty is that 340 students have already made arrangements around a September date — employment contracts, travel, and in at least forty documented cases, the only paid work available to them in the year.
A rule announced after people have organised their lives around its predecessor is not a rule but a penalty, and it falls hardest on exactly the students the faculty says it wants to retain.

The faculty's response — that the change benefits students on average — is true and beside the point. An average benefit does not license an individual cost imposed without notice, and no faculty would accept the same reasoning applied to its own staff contracts.
Make a specific demand of a named body
The Academic Board should apply the change from the next academic year and offer a September sitting this year to any student who requests it in writing before 30 June.
The cost of that concession is one additional sitting. The cost of the alternative is the faculty's ability to announce anything without being disbelieved.

seeds.goal: You can write a feature: open on a scene, move between the particular and the general, use one person's experience as evidence without letting it stand for everything, and land the argument.
seeds.why: Feature writing is where structure becomes invisible. The reader should feel they are being told a story while being given an argument.
seeds.ex: Aisha's feature about a closing rail halt was reprinted twice; the argument is in paragraph nine and nobody notices it arriving.
seeds.read: Read the feature and find one thing: where does the argument first appear?
seeds.task: Write a long-form feature opening (280–320 words): a scene, the person at its centre, the wider pattern with data, the argument, a complicating voice and a close that returns to the scene.
model: The 06:14 to Almaty stops at Uzynagash for forty seconds, and for thirty of them nobody moves.
Then Gulnara Sadykova, who has taught mathematics in the village school for twenty-six years, walks the length of the platform to the third carriage, because that is where the door will open.
She has done this four days a week since the halt at her end of the village closed in 2021, which added nineteen minutes to a journey she has made since she was twenty-three.

Ninety-one rural halts have closed in the country since 2018. The stated reason in each case is usage: a halt serving fewer than a set number of passengers a day is judged uneconomic and removed from the timetable.

The number, however, is counted after the service has been reduced. A halt served by two trains a day is used by fewer people than one served by six, and the count that closes it records the consequence of the previous decision rather than the demand for the halt.
In the eleven cases where the intermediate figures survive, usage fell by an average of 46 per cent in the two years between the reduction and the closure.

The regional operator does not dispute this. Its position, put plainly by a manager who asked not to be named, is that the alternative is not six trains but none: the line survives because the loss-making halts were removed.

Gulnara Sadykova has heard this argument and considers it separately from her own case. She will retire in four years. The teacher who replaces her will decide whether to move to the village on the basis of a timetable that now begins at 06:14 and involves a nineteen-minute walk in the dark.

seeds.goal: You can write a motivation letter for a competitive programme: connect a specific trajectory to a specific institution and say what you will do with what they give you.

model: Open with the trajectory, not the enthusiasm
I am applying to the MSc in Environmental Data Science because a project I ran badly showed me exactly what I do not yet know.
For eighteen months I collected water-quality readings from twelve points on the Ile river with two colleagues, using equipment we borrowed and calibrated ourselves.

We produced a dataset that is probably the densest available for that stretch and an analysis that I would now not defend: we treated readings from different instruments as comparable and ignored autocorrelation entirely.
Say what you learned from it
The data survived; the conclusions did not. What I took from it is that fieldwork discipline and statistical discipline are the same discipline applied at different points.
Give the specific reason for this institution

I am applying here specifically because of the sensor-network group and, within it, the work on calibration drift in low-cost instruments — which is the failure my own project ran into and could not diagnose.

I have read the two papers on the Danube network and understand that the method requires reference stations we do not have in our region, which is one of the questions I would like to work on.
What I would bring is the field side: two years of practical experience of what fails in a river in February, and a dataset with known, documented flaws that is available to the group.

Afterwards I intend to return: the country has fourteen monitoring stations for a river basin the size of a European country, and the constraint is not equipment but people who can defend an analysis.

seeds.goal: You can write a tribute: describe a person through what they did rather than through adjectives, admit what was difficult, and say what remains.
seeds.why: Tributes fail by generalising. The reader believes 'she never let a student leave without an answer' and disbelieves 'she was dedicated'.
seeds.ex: Alua's tribute to a retiring teacher was read aloud at the ceremony; two former students recognised themselves in it.
seeds.read: Read the tribute and find one thing: what difficult trait does the writer admit?
seeds.task: Write a tribute (240–280 words) to someone who is retiring or has been honoured: how you know them, three specific things they did, one honest difficulty, what changed because of them and what remains.
model: Zaure Bekovna leaves the school in June after thirty-one years, twenty-six of them teaching chemistry in the same room.
I was in her class for four years and worked as her laboratory assistant for two, which meant arriving at half past seven and learning that a lesson is mostly preparation.
She kept a wooden box of failed experiments on the top shelf, and used them: the burnt filter paper from 2011 explained more about heat control than any diagram.
She answered questions after the bell. Not sometimes — as a rule so consistent that students from other classes came to the door at ten past three and were not surprised to find her there.
In 2019, when the school had no money for reagents, she rewrote a term of practical work around materials available in a supermarket, and the results were better, which she found irritating.

seeds.goal: You can write a risk memo: state the risk, its likelihood and impact, the trigger that would confirm it, the mitigation and what you need decided.
seeds.why: Risks are usually raised too late and too vaguely. A memo that names a trigger converts an anxiety into a decision.

seeds.read: Read the memo and find one thing: what is the trigger that would confirm the risk?

model: State the risk in one sentence
There is a material risk that the migration will not complete before the academic year begins, and that we will run two systems in parallel for a term.
Say why you are raising it now
I am raising this now rather than at the next review because the last date on which a decision to rescope is cheap falls on 14 June.

Of the eleven modules scheduled for migration, four are complete and two of the remaining seven depend on an interface that has not been specified. On the current rate, completion falls in mid-September rather than late August.

Running in parallel is not a neutral outcome: it requires double entry of enrolment data by the registry, which in the last parallel period produced a discrepancy rate of about 3 per cent and four weeks of reconciliation.

The trigger to watch is the interface specification. If it is not signed off by 7 June, the two dependent modules cannot be tested before the freeze, and the September date becomes the expected outcome rather than the risk.
Give the first mitigation with cost

The first mitigation is to rescope: migrate the four complete modules and the three independent ones now, and defer the rest to January. This costs the benefit of a single cut-over and removes the parallel period entirely.

The second is to add contractor capacity for six weeks, at approximately 4.5 million tenge, which the current rate suggests would recover about half the gap and does not address the specification dependency at all.
The decision I need by 14 June is which of these we are doing. If no decision is made, we are choosing the parallel period by default, and I would rather that were chosen deliberately.

seeds.goal: You can review a literature: organise studies by argument rather than by date, show where they disagree and why, and identify the gap your work addresses.
seeds.why: A list of studies is not a review. The organising question is: what does this field disagree about, and what would settle it?

seeds.read: Read the review and find one thing: what gap does the writer identify?
seeds.task: Write a short literature review (280–320 words) on a research question: organise the work into positions, show the disagreement and its source, note methodological differences and identify the gap.
model: State the question the literature addresses
Research on class size divides on a question that is empirical in form and methodological in substance: whether reductions in class size produce attainment gains large enough to justify their cost.
The first position, associated with the Tennessee STAR experiment and its successors, reports substantial and durable effects, particularly for younger and disadvantaged students.
The second, drawing largely on administrative data from Europe and East Asia, reports effects close to zero once teacher assignment is controlled for.
Locate the source of the disagreement

The disagreement is not primarily about the data but about what a class-size reduction is. In the experimental literature it is an exogenous change with staffing held constant; in the administrative literature it is typically the result of a policy that also changed who was teaching.

A third group treats this explicitly, arguing that class-size effects are real but conditional: they appear where the reduction is accompanied by a change in what the teacher does with the smaller group, and vanish where the lesson format is unchanged.
Give the evidence for the third
The strongest support comes from studies with classroom observation, which are rare: of the fifteen studies reviewed here, four observed lessons, and all four report the conditional pattern.

The methodological division tracks the substantive one almost exactly, which is itself a finding: fields in which the measurement determines the answer are fields in which the question has not yet been specified.

What is missing is a study in which class size is reduced without any accompanying instruction on how to teach the smaller class, and lessons are observed. Such a design is unattractive to funders and is precisely the one that would settle the dispute.

seeds.goal: You can write an argument from data: describe what the data show, distinguish what they establish from what they suggest, and resist the conclusion they do not support.
seeds.why: The commonest failure in data writing is a conclusion one step beyond the evidence. Marking that step visibly is the skill.

seeds.read: Read the essay and find one thing: which conclusion does the writer refuse to draw?
seeds.task: Write an essay built on data (260–300 words) about a trend you can describe: the pattern, the obvious explanation, why it is insufficient, a better one, what the data cannot establish and a conclusion.
model: Between 2015 and 2023, the share of school leavers in our region entering higher education rose from 41 to 58 per cent, while the share completing a degree within six years rose only from 34 to 38.
The gap between entry and completion therefore widened from seven percentage points to twenty, and almost all of the widening occurred after 2019.
The obvious reading is that expansion admitted weaker students: if entry grows faster than capability, completion must fall behind.
This cannot be the whole account. Entry examination scores of admitted students fell by less than three points over the period, and the fall occurred mainly in 2016–17, before the widening began.

A better fit is the change in what students were admitted to. The growth is concentrated almost entirely in fee-paying places on programmes with the highest reported withdrawal for financial reasons, and the timing matches: the widening begins in the year those places expanded.
Withdrawal data support this indirectly: reported reasons shift over the period from academic to financial, and the shift is concentrated in exactly those programmes.
State what the data cannot establish
What these data cannot establish is causation. Reported reasons for withdrawal are self-described, financial and academic difficulty are correlated, and no student in this dataset is observed twice.

The defensible conclusion is therefore narrower than the interesting one: the widening gap is unlikely to be explained by admitting weaker students, and any policy built on that assumption is being built on a reading the data do not support.

seeds.goal: You can write about a live controversy: represent each side as its holders would, identify what is actually at stake, and be clear about where you stand without caricature.
seeds.why: Writing about controversy is where fairness and honesty pull apart. Fairness is not neutrality; it is accuracy about people you disagree with.
seeds.ex: Aliya's article was cited by both sides of the dispute it described, which is the only real test.
seeds.read: Read the article and find one thing: what does the writer say is actually at stake?
seeds.task: Write an article about a controversy (280–320 words): the occasion, each side stated as its holders would state it, what is actually at stake beneath the argument, the weakest point on each side and your own position.
model: The decision to teach the history of the 1930s from a single approved textbook has produced a dispute that both sides describe as being about accuracy, and that is not about accuracy.

Those who support the change argue, reasonably, that a subject taught from twelve competing textbooks cannot be examined fairly, and that the previous arrangement made a student's result depend on which school they attended.

Those who oppose it argue, equally reasonably, that a single official account of a contested period converts a historical question into a civic one, and that the value of the subject lies precisely in the disagreement.

Both positions are held by people who teach the subject, and both are supported by the same observation: that most students currently learn the period as a set of dates because the disagreement is too difficult to examine.
Say what is actually at stake

What is actually at stake is not the textbook but the examination. A subject assessed by recall requires a single account; a subject assessed by argument does not, and can survive twelve textbooks or none.
Name the weak point on the first side
The weakness of the official position is that it treats the examination as fixed, which is the one element the ministry controls entirely.
Name the weak point on the second
The weakness of the opposing position is that it defends a plurality that most schools were not using: eight of the twelve textbooks were in use in fewer than five per cent of classrooms.

My own view is that the dispute is being conducted about the wrong object, and that both sides would accept the other's arrangement if the assessment changed first. That is not a compromise; it is a claim that the argument has been mislabelled by everybody, including the people making it well.

seeds.goal: You can write the narrative section of a funding application: the problem, why existing work does not solve it, your approach, feasibility, and what the money buys.
seeds.why: Funders read for feasibility and specificity. A brilliant idea with no plan for the first six months is indistinguishable from an ambition.
seeds.ex: Miras's application named what the first 100,000 tenge would be spent on. The panel's comment: 'unusually concrete'.
seeds.read: Read the narrative and find one thing: what will be delivered in the first six months?
seeds.task: Write a grant narrative (280–320 words): the problem with evidence, why existing approaches fail, your approach, why you can do it, the first six months, and what the funding buys.
model: Seventeen of the twenty-three district hospitals in the region have no functioning system for tracking which patients have missed follow-up appointments, and the consequence is measurable: in the two hospitals that do track this, re-admission within ninety days is a third lower.

The standard solution — a regional information system — has been attempted twice and abandoned twice, in both cases for the same reason: it required data entry by clinical staff during consultations, which did not happen and was never going to.

This project takes the opposite approach: it does not add a system but reads one that already exists. Appointment scheduling is already digital in all twenty-three hospitals; missed appointments are therefore already recorded and simply never queried.

The work consists of a weekly extraction from the existing scheduling database, a rule for identifying clinically significant misses agreed with two consultants, and a single printed list delivered to each department — deliberately not a dashboard, because dashboards are not read.
Say why you can do it

The approach has been tested in one hospital for four months, where 61 per cent of listed patients were contacted within a week and 44 per cent attended a rescheduled appointment. The extraction script exists and the two consultants have agreed to formalise the rule.

In the first six months the project will extend the extraction to six hospitals, publish the rule so that others can adopt or dispute it, and produce comparative re-admission figures for the participating sites.

The requested 4.8 million tenge buys one data analyst at 0.5 FTE for a year, the printing and delivery costs, and two days a month of consultant time for the rule review. It buys no software licences, and none are required.

The principal risk is that hospitals treat the list as an audit rather than as a tool; the mitigation, learned from the pilot, is that the list is addressed to the department and never to the administration.

seeds.goal: You can write a strategy memo: state the choice, the reasoning, what is being given up, what would change your mind and the first decision.
seeds.why: A strategy that gives nothing up is a wish list. Naming the sacrifice is what makes a memo a strategy.

seeds.read: Read the memo and find one thing: what is being given up?
seeds.task: Write a strategy memo (260–300 words): the situation, the choice recommended, the reasoning, what is explicitly given up, what would change your mind and the first decision required.
model: We currently run three product lines with one engineering team of nine, and each line receives roughly a third of the capacity and grows at roughly a third of the rate it could.
The recommendation is to concentrate two thirds of engineering capacity on the analytics line for the next four quarters, and to hold the other two lines at maintenance.

The reasoning is not that analytics is the largest line; it is not. It is that it is the only line where our win rate rises with product depth: in the last eight competitive evaluations, we lost six on features that require sustained work rather than on price.
The other two lines lose on price and on integrations, neither of which engineering capacity fixes at our scale.
Say plainly what is given up

What we are giving up is explicit and should be stated in the meeting rather than discovered later: the reporting line will not gain the two features requested by our three largest customers this year, and at least one of them is likely to leave at renewal.
That is approximately 11 per cent of current revenue, and the recommendation stands only if we are prepared to lose it deliberately rather than argue about it in October.
Say what would change your mind

Two things would change this recommendation: if the next four competitive evaluations show us losing analytics deals on price rather than depth, the concentration is misdirected; and if maintenance mode on the other lines produces support load above 20 per cent of capacity, the arithmetic does not work.

The decision required this month is the reallocation itself. Everything else — hiring, the renewal conversation with the reporting customers, the roadmap — follows from it and cannot sensibly be decided first.

seeds.goal: You can write a speech: build in the repetition, rhythm and signposting that a listener needs, and end on a line that survives being heard once.
seeds.why: Written prose read aloud fails: a listener cannot re-read. Writing for the ear means redundancy is a feature, not a fault.
seeds.ex: Damir's five-minute speech used one repeated phrase. It is the only part anybody quoted afterwards.
seeds.read: Read the speech and find one thing: which phrase is repeated, and how many times?
seeds.task: Write a speech (260–300 words) for a school-leaving ceremony: open with something concrete, signpost the structure, use one repeated phrase, include one story, address the audience directly and end on a line that survives being heard once.
model: In the corridor outside room 214 there is a mark on the wall, about a metre and a half up, where eleven years of school bags have hit the same brick.
I want to say three things about that mark, and then I will sit down, which is a promise and also a structure.
The first is that none of us made it. It was made by all of us, one bag at a time, and not one of those collisions was intentional.
That is what a school is: a thing nobody makes on purpose.

In year eight our class spent four months arguing about whether to enter the debating competition. We entered on the last possible day, lost in the first round to a school we had never heard of, and eleven of us are still friends because of those four months of arguing.
The second thing is that we were wrong about which parts mattered. Nobody in this hall remembers a single mark from year nine. Everybody remembers who sat next to them.

The third is for the teachers, and it is short: you spent eleven years being interrupted by us, and you kept answering. That is what a school is — a thing nobody makes on purpose, made by people who turn up anyway.

The mark on the wall will still be there in September, and by October there will be new bags hitting it. That is not sad. That is the whole point.

seeds.goal: You can escalate beyond an organisation: set out the chronology, show that internal remedies are exhausted, cite the rule breached and state the outcome sought.
seeds.why: A regulator reads dozens of these. Yours succeeds if it can be assessed without asking you a single question.
seeds.ex: Aigerim's escalation attached a numbered chronology and nothing else. The regulator opened a case in nine days.
seeds.read: Read the escalation and find one thing: which rule does the writer say has been breached?
seeds.task: Write an escalation to a regulator (260–300 words): the parties, the chronology with dates, the rule breached, why internal remedies are exhausted, the outcome sought and the documents enclosed.
model: Open formally and identify the parties
Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to refer a matter concerning Aktau Telecom LLP, account 55-0912, which I have been unable to resolve directly.
Summarise the matter in one sentence

seeds.goal: You can write an essay about film that argues rather than reviews: take a claim about how films work, test it against specific sequences, and admit where it breaks.

model: A flashback works when it withholds information the present scene has already made the audience want, and fails when it supplies information the audience has not yet learned to need.
The mechanism is attention: a flashback interrupts, and an interruption is tolerated only if it answers a question that is already open.

'The Godfather Part II' opens its Sicilian sequences only after the present-day Michael has become inexplicable to the audience — we have watched him do something we cannot square with the man in the first film, and the past arrives as an answer to a question we are already asking.

'Casablanca' is the standard case for the opposite reason: the Paris flashback lasts three minutes and arrives at the precise moment Rick's behaviour has become inexplicable to Ilsa and to us. Cut it earlier and it is exposition; cut it later and the film has already answered itself.
The claim runs into trouble with 'Rashomon', where the flashbacks arrive before any question has been raised, and the film works.

It would be possible to say that the question in 'Rashomon' is raised by the framing device. I do not think that survives contact with the film: the framing device establishes a situation, not a question, and the first flashback begins before the audience has any reason to doubt anybody.
Revise the claim rather than abandon it
What the counter-example forces is a narrower claim: the mechanism holds for flashbacks that explain a character, and not for flashbacks whose subject is the unreliability of explanation itself.
That narrowing is not a retreat. A rule that covers character flashbacks and openly excludes the epistemological ones is more useful than a rule that covers everything by covering nothing.

seeds.goal: You can write a position paper: state a collective position, ground it in principle and evidence, address the strongest opposing interest and say what you are asking for.
seeds.why: A position paper speaks for a group to people with power. It must be defensible by anyone in the group, which rules out the writer's private flourishes.

model: The Students' Association opposes the introduction of proctoring software for online examinations, and proposes an alternative that meets the same objective.
Our position rests on a principle rather than on convenience: monitoring should be proportionate to the risk it addresses and should not extend into spaces the institution does not otherwise enter.
Give the evidence on the risk

The stated risk is impersonation and unauthorised assistance. In the last three years, thirteen cases have been substantiated across roughly 60,000 online assessments, and eleven of the thirteen were detected by the marking process rather than by any monitoring.
Give the evidence on the cost

The proposed system requires continuous camera and screen access in students' homes, retains recordings for ninety days, and, in the pilot, produced 340 flags of which 4 were upheld — a false-positive rate that transfers the burden of proof to the student.

The institution's interest is not illegitimate: a degree that cannot be defended against the claim of unassessed learning loses value for the students who hold it, and that argument is made by graduates as often as by administrators.

We therefore propose assessment redesign rather than surveillance: for the eleven modules where the risk is concentrated, a short oral verification of the submitted work, sampled at 10 per cent and applied to all students equally.
Address the cost of the alternative
This is not free: it requires approximately 90 staff hours per semester. It is, however, less than the estimated licence cost of the proctoring system and it produces a defensible record.
State what you are asking for
We ask the Senate to defer the procurement decision by one semester and to pilot oral verification in three modules, with the Association contributing student time to schedule the sessions.

seeds.goal: You can evaluate a programme formally: restate the theory of change, test each link, distinguish outputs from outcomes and judge whether the programme should continue.
seeds.why: Evaluations fail when they measure activity. Testing the causal chain — and saying which link broke — is what makes them useful.
seeds.ex: Zhanel's evaluation found the programme delivered every output and no outcome. The finding changed the design.
seeds.read: Read the evaluation and find one thing: which link in the chain failed?
seeds.task: Write an evaluation report (280–320 words): the programme's theory of change, what was delivered, what changed, which link failed, alternative explanations considered and a judgement.
model: This evaluation covers the first two years of the rural mentoring programme, funded from the regional education budget.

The programme's logic was explicit: pairing final-year school students with university mentors would raise application rates to selective universities, by supplying information about the process that is unavailable in schools with no recent applicants.
Delivery was strong. 214 pairs were formed against a target of 200; 78 per cent of pairs met at least eight times; mentor retention was 91 per cent.

Outcomes were not. Applications to selective universities from participating schools rose from 34 to 39, against a rise from 31 to 36 in matched non-participating schools — a difference well inside the variation between years.

The link that failed is the second one. Participants report substantially better knowledge of the application process — a 41-point rise on the knowledge questions — and no corresponding change in intention. Information was delivered; it did not convert.

Interviews suggest why. The barrier named by participants is not knowledge but cost and distance: 68 per cent named the price of relocation, and mentoring cannot address it. The programme's theory assumed an information problem in a population with a financial one.
Two alternative explanations were tested and do not hold: the effect is not hidden by cohort size, and it is not delayed, since the first cohort has now completed the application cycle.

The programme should not continue in its current form. It is well run and it works on the wrong variable. The mentoring infrastructure, however, is functioning and could be redirected: mentors are already trusted, and a bursary application is exactly the kind of task that fails for want of a person who has done it before.

seeds.goal: You can negotiate formally in writing: acknowledge the other position, state your constraint, propose a package rather than a demand, and keep a route to agreement open.
seeds.why: Written negotiation freezes positions. The craft is proposing something the other side can accept without appearing to have lost.

seeds.task: Write a negotiating letter (260–300 words): acknowledge their position, state your constraint honestly, propose a package with more than one variable, name what you cannot move, and keep the route open.
model: Thank you for your letter of 4 March. I understand the position it sets out, and I do not think it is unreasonable: a fixed fee protects you against a project that expands, and your experience of that expansion is presumably the reason the clause exists.

My difficulty is not the fee itself but its combination with an open scope. As drafted, the agreement fixes my payment and leaves the volume of work to be determined by a party that has no reason to limit it.
State the principle you are working from
I would rather solve that with a mechanism than with a higher number, because a higher number does not fix the problem; it only prices a risk that neither of us can currently estimate.

I therefore propose three changes together, and I am flexible on which of them we use. First, a defined scope schedule attached to the agreement. Second, a rate for work beyond that schedule, which need not be high. Third, if you prefer to keep the fee entirely fixed, a cap on revisions of three rounds per deliverable.

Any two of these would resolve my concern. If the schedule is difficult to define in advance — and it may genuinely be — the revision cap alone would be sufficient, and it is the change that costs you least.
The one point I cannot move on is the payment schedule: 50 per cent on signature is not negotiable, because it is what makes the project possible for me to take at all.
In return, I am content to remove the termination clause I proposed, which you objected to and which I included largely out of habit.

If none of these works, I would rather hear that than negotiate by exchange of drafts: a fifteen-minute call would probably settle it. I remain glad to do this project. Yours sincerely, Ruslan Aitkhozhin.

seeds.goal: You can answer a professional question in public: establish what the asker needs, answer it directly, qualify where the answer depends, and say what you would need to know to be more precise.
seeds.why: Expert answers fail by answering a more interesting question than the one asked. Discipline here is a form of respect.

seeds.read: Read the reply and find one thing: what does the writer say they would need to know to be more precise?
seeds.task: Write an expert reply (240–280 words) to a professional question: restate what is being asked, give the direct answer, explain why, name the conditions under which it changes, correct a common misconception and say what you would need to know.
model: As I read it, the question is whether you should index the timestamp column, given that your queries filter on a date range and sort by the same column.
Yes, and specifically a single index on (tenant_id, created_at) rather than on created_at alone.

Your filter is always scoped to one tenant, and a composite index in that order lets the database seek to the tenant and then scan a contiguous range, which also satisfies the sort without a separate sorting step.

This holds as long as tenant_id is selective — that is, as long as no single tenant holds most of the rows. If one tenant is 80 per cent of the table, the index will not help that tenant's queries at all, and their queries are presumably the ones you care about.
It also assumes your write volume is moderate. Every index is paid for on insert, and on a table taking several thousand rows a second the cost is not negligible.

One thing worth flagging: adding created_at as a second index in addition will not help and will cost you. The composite index already serves queries that filter on tenant_id alone; it does not serve queries that filter on created_at alone, and if you have those, they are a different problem.
The quickest way to check all of this on your own data is to look at the execution plan before and after on a copy — not on the assumption that it will behave as described here.
Say what you would need to know

To be more precise I would need to know the row distribution across tenants and whether the sort is ascending or descending in the common case, because a descending sort on some engines does not use an ascending index efficiently.

tl.long: It is important to note at this point that the evidence which the author presents is not conclusive.
tl.model: The author's evidence is not conclusive.
tl.why: 'It is important to note at this point' announces instead of arguing.

tl.long: Despite the fact that the argument is presented in a very convincing manner, it rests on one single study.
tl.model: Convincing as it is, the argument rests on one study.
tl.why: Concession can be carried by structure rather than by a phrase.

tl.long: There is a tendency on the part of policymakers to make the assumption that money solves the problem.
tl.model: Policymakers tend to assume that money solves the problem.
tl.why: Verbs buried in nouns make prose slow: tend, assume.

tl.long: The reason for the failure of the programme was the fact that nobody had been trained to run it.
tl.model: The programme failed because nobody was trained to run it.
tl.why: 'The reason for the failure was the fact that' is six words for because.

tl.long: In the event that further funding becomes available, the pilot could be extended to other regions.
tl.model: If further funding appears, the pilot could extend to other regions.
tl.why: 'In the event that' is legal boilerplate, not argument.

tl.long: It cannot be denied that there exists a considerable degree of disagreement among the researchers.
tl.why: Double negatives plus abstract nouns bury a simple fact.

tl.long: The author makes an attempt to provide an explanation for the decline in participation rates.
tl.model: The author tries to explain the decline in participation.
tl.why: Make an attempt to provide an explanation = try to explain.

tl.long: With regard to the question of cost, it must be said that no figures at all are given.
tl.model: On cost, the report gives no figures.
tl.why: 'With regard to the question of' is throat-clearing.

tl.long: The final chapter, which is the shortest one in the whole book, deals with the practical consequences.
tl.model: The final and shortest chapter deals with practical consequences.
tl.why: A relative clause becomes an adjective.

tl.long: It would appear to be the case that the two studies are measuring quite different things entirely.
tl.model: The two studies appear to measure different things.
tl.why: Three hedges stacked on one another cancel out.

offIdeas: A summary of the whole text instead of a response
Summary crowds out the analysis the genre exists for.
Unanchored praise is indistinguishable from padding.
A biographical fact about the author
Biography explains nothing about the argument's validity.
A claim about what most readers will feel
You cannot evidence other readers' reactions.
One controlling idea per text is the price of coherence.
A digression into your own experience
The genre licenses judgement, not memoir.
A proposal without a mechanism is a wish.
An appeal to how urgent the topic is
Urgency is a substitute for argument, not a form of it.

outlineRules.msg: The thesis may open the text, but the recommendation cannot: it has to be earned by the evidence between them.
A conclusion that introduces evidence admits that the body of the text was incomplete.

rubric.task: Does the text answer the exact question, hold one position, and address the strongest objection to it?
rubric.organisation: Paragraphs that each do one job, with the logic visible at the joins.
rubric.vocabulary: Register held consistently; collocation and connotation controlled, not merely varied.
rubric.grammar: Subordination, inversion, nominalisation and hedging used for effect rather than for display.
